items.question: Why do you have reservations about relying on a new regulatory regime to manage advanced AI?
items.object: AI regulation and the analogy between the FDA and AI oversight
items.answer: I think the fundamental thing to think about here is really assumptions. There are many worlds in which humans can thrive amid things that are better than them at various kinds of intellectual tasks. And I just have very serious issues with the idea we're just going to be able to pass a new regulatory regime and everything's going to go fine and there will be no side effects. And these analogies of FDA to AI are not really very good. It's not to say that I don't think we need something like an FDA.

There are many worlds in which humans can thrive amid things that are better than them at various kinds of intellectual tasks. And I just have very serious issues with the idea we're just going to be able to pass a new regulatory regime and everything's going to go fine and there will be no side effects. And these analogies of FDA to AI are not really very good. It's not to say that I don't think we need something like an FDA.

The response questions the assumption that introducing a new AI regulatory regime will ensure that everything goes well.
The response judges the FDA analogy for AI regulation to be weak.

items.question: How do you expect major AI companies to respond to a model that seems to pose a risk of overthrowing the US government?
items.object: Major AI companies' willingness to release models that threaten the US government
items.answer: I just kind of have this sneaking suspicion that if the models seemed like they were going to pose the risk of overthrowing the US government or anything in that vicinity, I don't think OpenAI would release that model or Anthropic or Meta or XAI or Google. I just don't think they would.
quotes: I just kind of have this sneaking suspicion that if the models seemed like they were going to pose the risk of overthrowing the US government or anything in that vicinity, I don't think Open AAI would release that model or Anthropic or Meta or XAI or Google. I just don't think they would.

rubrics.text: The response expresses the expectation that major AI companies would refrain from releasing a model that appeared to pose a risk of overthrowing the US government.

items.question: Why do you think developing superintelligence should require scientific consensus on safety and strong public buy-in?
items.object: The Future of Life Institute’s proposed prohibition on developing superintelligence without scientific safety consensus and public buy-in
items.answer: Well, if you negate that statement, then you're saying that we should be allowed to go ahead and build artificial super intelligence even if there's no real consensus at all that it can be kept under control or that people even want it. Right? And if we were to say that then we would be basically doing the most spectacular corporate welfare, because we don't do that in any other industries. Right now there are more regulations on sandwiches than super intelligence in the US. If you want to sell drugs, medicines, cars, airplanes, you always have to demonstrate to the satisfaction of some independent scientists who don't have a conflict of interest that this is safe enough. The benefits outweigh the harms. I'm just saying we should treat super intelligence the same way. And right now 95% of all Americans in a new poll don't actually want to race to super intelligence. And most scientists who work on this agree that we have no clue at the moment how to keep something which is so vastly smarter than us under control.

items.question: How would you design AI safety regulation without having to define superintelligence?
items.object: AI safety regulation based on harms rather than a definition of superintelligence
items.answer:
I think it's actually quite easy to write this law, and I don't think it requires defining super intelligence at all. Let me explain a little bit what I mean by that. If we treat AI like we treat any other industry that makes powerful tech, we would then have safety standards, right? There are safety standards for restaurants; before they can open, they have to have someone check the kitchen. So, if you had safety standards for AI, they wouldn't need to define super intelligence. You might want to demonstrate that it's not going to teach terrorists how to make bioweapons. If it's a very powerful system, you probably put one of the safety standards as having to demonstrate that you can keep this under control. If the company selling it can't convincingly make the case that this thing is not going to cause the overthrow of the US government, then reject, you know, come back when you can. I didn't mention super intelligence here at all. It's the company's obligation to demonstrate that they meet the standards.

To take an analogy that might help clarify what I'm talking about here, let's talk about thalidomide for a little bit. The dumb way to prevent such harm would have been if the FDA had a special rule that we have a ban on medicines that cause babies to be born without arms or legs. What if someone comes out with a new medicine now and the arms and legs are fine, but the baby has no kidneys or no brain? That's not the way to go about it. The way you instead go about it is you ask the companies to do a clinical trial and provide quantitative evidence of all the different side effects that people might not want. Quantify them, how many percent get each, and then quantify the benefits. You give this to some independent experts who don't have money on the line so they can't work for the companies, for example, who look at the benefits and the harms and they decide: is this a net positive for the American people? Then they approve it. This is how we do regulations in all other areas, and this is how I think it's quite easy to do also for AI. You don't define super intelligence; you just define the harms that society is not okay with. Broadly, it boils down to demonstrating that the harms are small enough to be acceptable, and then it's the company's job to make all the definitions they want, quantify things, and persuade these independent experts.

items.question: How do you think safety-case regulation should shape companies' technical decisions?
items.object: Safety-case regulation and market-driven innovation
items.answer: I think what the companies need to demonstrate in the safety case is a high level thing. The government wants to know how many flight hours on average do you have until a failure, and so on. If the companies can solve that whatever way they want, it's in the interest of the companies to not use flaky manufacturers, to have good procedures and have people study crack formation, the physics of it, and so on. Then they'll switch to another alloy if that works better. It's the same for medicines. The government doesn't come in and micromanage, "Oh, this chemical is allowed, this ingredient is not allowed." Rather, the company, if they have an effect, some medicine that seems to be pretty good at—suppose there's a new antibiotic that seems really good against bronchitis—it contains lead and aluminum and cyanide in small doses. People will look in the company and be like, "We're having a hard time demonstrating the safety of lead. Maybe this works even without the lead. Maybe we can swap out this thing." So all the innovation is driven by capitalism, by market forces.

items.question: Why do you see nuclear reactor regulation as a good example of quantitative safety requirements that allow innovation?
items.object: Quantitative safety requirements for nuclear reactors
items.answer: I think nuclear reactors are a great example, because what the law actually says there is the company has to make a real quantitative calculation and demonstrate that the risk of a meltdown is less than one in 10,000 years to even get permission to start building it. The company has free reign to come up with whatever reactor design they want, and then they will innovate, and whoever you first meet, though, is going to get the big bucks.
quotes: Nuclear reactors are a great example, because what the law actually says there is the company has to make a real quantitative calculation and demonstrate that the risk of a meltdown is less than one in 10,000 years to even get permission to start building it.

rubrics.text: The response states that permission to begin building a nuclear reactor requires demonstrating a meltdown risk below one in 10,000 years.
The response identifies nuclear reactor regulation as allowing companies to choose any reactor design that meets the quantitative safety requirement.

items.question: How do you view the argument that an AI company would face common-law liability if releasing superintelligence caused human extinction?
items.object: Common-law liability for harms caused by superintelligence
items.answer: Well, human extinction, sure. But I'm sort of skeptical that that's what we're going to have on day one. That company is subject to common law liability, and there are common law—if we're all extinct.

items.object: Evidence for AI-caused human extinction
items.answer: A lot of people talk about extinction too, wouldn't you say? I mean, a lot of people do, but there still is not the kind of persuasive evidence for extinction in terms of not just theoretically, but mechanically, how would that work? I just don't think we've seen that to nearly the same extent that we have.

items.question: Why do you think AI models are a difficult unit of regulation?
items.object: AI models as a unit of regulation
items.answer: I think, as a practical matter, the issue that you have is that those things are bits, and it's very hard to just purely regulate bits. Instead of imposing regulations at the layer of the model, which is a really difficult layer of abstraction on which to do it, it's the same way that we don't tend to place regulations at the layer of computers or software or transistors. These are really important general-purpose technologies that undoubtedly all three of those things have killed lots of people at this point. We don't regulate at that layer of abstraction because it's not very practical. It's not a good unit of abstraction and not a good conceptual unit of account for regulation. When it comes to safety standards for something like a generalist artificial intelligence model, I think in the long run we will build those standards. I don't think anybody in the spectrum is saying that there won't be standards for safety, security, et cetera, of large language models.

items.question: How do you think physical safeguards can address biological risks created by AI?
items.object: Physical safeguards against biological risks from AI
items.answer: You can do essentially automated gain-of-function research with a nucleic acid language model today. You can basically simulate the evolutionary process that allows for more virulent viruses or whatever else, and we've seen the early stages of this from people like the Arc Institute in California. Those are not ChatGPT-style models, but it's the same architecture trained on nucleic acid sequences, right? So we know that's a thing. There are all these choke points in the physical world. Some of them are labs of certain biosafety level categories, BSL-3 and -4. Some of it is at the layer of nucleic acid synthesis screening, which, basically, you have to say, if you're going to order the creation of a certain kind of nucleic acid, we're going to, as a matter of policy, require that you screen that against some methodology that allows us to test whether or not you're trying to make a pathogen. I worked on some of those policies when I was in the Trump administration. These are all things that we do. Those are safety standards that exist, that are emerging, that are downstream in many ways of advancements in AI. I think the urgency of policies like nucleic acid synthesis screening goes up because of AI.

items.question: How do you understand the United States’ traditional approach to addressing harms from new technologies?
items.object: The United States’ traditional approach to governing new technologies and addressing their harms
items.answer: I think the broader point here is that this is traditionally the way that we do things in the United States: you build a technology, you gain experience in practice with its utility, and you diffuse it throughout the economy in this very complicated way. Sometimes there are demonstrated harms, and when there are demonstrated harms, the first thing we do is deal with that through the liability system. I would point out that OpenAI, Google, and other companies have common-law liability, not copyright cases, but "you caused physical harm to me" type of liability cases against them for chatbots, right?

Sometimes there are demonstrated harms, and when there are demonstrated harms, the first thing we do is deal with that through the liability system.

items.question: Why do you think the traditional approach of learning from technological mistakes becomes inadequate for artificial superintelligence?
items.object: Learning from mistakes as a strategy for regulating artificial superintelligence
items.answer: I completely agree that this is how things have been done in the past: let technologies come up, people invent the car, a bunch of people die, and then gradually you mandate the seat belt, traffic lights, speed limits, and other things to make the product safer. But it's important to remember that science has been getting progressively more powerful from ancient times until now, and as a result technology also keeps growing exponentially in its power. At some point the technology gets powerful enough that this old traditional strategy of just learning from mistakes goes from being a good strategy to being a bad one. I think it worked well for cars. It worked well for things like fire. We needed fire first. We didn't regulate it to death. Later we decided to put fire codes in and have fire extinguishers and fire trucks. I would argue that nuclear weapons are already above this threshold. We don't want to let everybody who wants to buy hydrogen bombs in supermarkets and then say, "Oopsie, that didn't go so well; we had nuclear winter and 99% of Americans starve to death." We already have a bunch of proactive laws about how to deal with hydrogen bombs. Even despite all your work in the government, you are not allowed to buy your own hydrogen bomb, even though I would trust you with it; I know you're a nice guy. I'm not allowed to start doing new plutonium research in my lab at MIT, even if I pinky-promise I'm going to be careful, just because one mistake there is viewed by society as one too many, and they know I don't have enough cash to pay the liability if I get sued afterwards. I would argue that artificial superintelligence is vastly more powerful in terms of the downside than hydrogen bombs would ever be. There have been some pretty careful calculations recently showing that only about 99% of all Americans would die and starve to death in the worst-case scenario if there's a global nuclear war with Russia, so there's still 3 million who survive. Whereas if we lose control of artificial superintelligence because somebody sloppily built a new robot species that took over, you know—

items.question: How do you distinguish the regulatory approach you favor for controllable AI tools from the approach you favor for artificial superintelligence?
items.object: Risk-based regulation of controllable AI tools and artificial superintelligence
items.answer: The way I see this is not that there's anything wrong with the traditional wisdom for how to regulate things. I think that's appropriate for all tech below a certain risk threshold. We're very lucky with AI that so many of the great benefits we have are not particularly risky. AlphaFold is an absolutely superhuman tool for folding proteins, great for drug discovery. Autonomous vehicles can save, I believe, over a million lives every year from pointless road deaths. There's so much productivity that can be gained from building controllable AI tools, and those—I think it's very feasible to continue having the liability system you're describing, the traditional way: learn from mistakes and then fix it. It's only fringe stuff, in particular artificial superintelligence, which is on the wrong side of that threshold where right now there's not much upside, frankly, to sprint to building superintelligence in three years. In my opinion, if we could do it safely in 20 years instead, we'd be much better off just doing controllable tools until then. That's why it irks me so much that people conflate these two things a lot. I'm not saying you do, but a lot of folks I've spoken to on the Hill do, and think the only choice we have is more AI or less AI, or go forward or stop. I see development as branching into two paths: either we continue going aggressively forward to build all these great tools but insist that companies demonstrate they are controllable tools, or go all in on building superintelligence.

items.question: Why did you think the AI action plan's omission of superintelligence and AGI was wise?
items.object: The AI action plan's omission of superintelligence and AGI
items.answer: I was so pleasantly surprised when I read the action plan that it didn't mention the word superintelligence a single time, not even AGI. I think that was really wise because it highlights that there's so much great stuff we can do with AI tools without having to get into the whole question of superintelligence.

items.question: What would make you willing to support an AI-model evaluation for human-extinction risk?
items.object: AI-model evaluations for human-extinction risk
items.answer: It's very hard to demonstrate in concrete ways what this looks like. To this point, if you could formulate what you wanted, if you could formulate affirmative technical, empirical things we could say about models—okay, we've stress-tested the model in this way, we've run this eval or done this thing, and shown that the model passes what we view as an acceptable threshold—then I would totally be willing to say, "Yeah, let's make that an eval." You don't even need to pass a law. Make it an eval. I promise you, if you made that an eval and got enough credible people around to support it, I think labs would probably just run it.

items.question: How do you think AI regulation should distinguish between different kinds of software?
items.object: Risk-based classes for AI regulation
items.answer: More broadly, with regulation of things, let's take drugs again: to not drown companies in red tape and stifle innovation, one tends to look at rough plausibility and divide all products into classes. We have class one drugs, class two, class three, class four. There are much higher safety standards for fentanyl or other new opioid drugs than for new cough medicines for adults or for new vitamins. If you take the same approach to AI, what would you say if there's some new software that translates English into Chinese or Japanese? The most embarrassing thing that could probably happen is a repeat of the Monty Python skit with a fake Hungarian dictionary.

items.question: Why do you think AI companies should have to make a safety case even when policymakers cannot predict exactly how superintelligence could harm people?
items.object: The burden of proof for demonstrating AI safety
items.answer: What we do in industry now is let companies make the safety case rather than the government. You said it's hard to foresee exactly how superintelligence, if it's smarter than all humans combined, would kill us all. Being a scientist for so many years has made me humble about these things. It would have been hard for the makers of thalidomide to predict that it would cause babies to be born without arms or legs when all it did was reduce nausea in their moms. We didn't understand how that would happen, but it did. Because of that, it would have been reasonable to say, we've noticed there are a lot of things that can cause birth defects; we don't understand exactly how it works, so before we try it on all American mothers with no prescription, let's try it on a small number of mothers and see what happens to their babies. You shift the burden of proof away from politicians having to articulate why this is dangerous and to the companies: we just have to do some basic research to make the safety case.

The response proposes small-scale empirical testing before widespread exposure as a way to assess harms whose mechanisms are not understood.

items.question: How would you expect an FDA-style regulator for AI to affect technological progress?
items.object: An FDA-style regulator for AI
items.answer: If we did this with AI today, if I had a magic wand and created an FDA for AI, you'd have class one, two, three, four, or AI safety level one, two, three, four systems, along the lines of what many AI companies already have in voluntary commitments. There would be very easy requirements for ASL-1 and so on. For the higher-level systems, companies would have to do a lot more to quantify the safety case. I think we'd end up in a golden age of AI progress, flooded with new medical treatments, amazing autonomous vehicles, and great increases in productivity. The one area that would get slowed down noticeably is the race to build actual superintelligence, where I think nobody would be able to make a safety case yet. If we have to wait 20 years to get that done properly, it's way better than racing to it and bungling it and squandering everything.

items.question: How do you assess the claim that FDA approval is required before potentially dangerous biological or medical products can be released?
items.object: Gaps in FDA oversight of biological and medical products
items.answer: Not quite. You can release CRISPR-engineered bacteria without consulting the FDA because those are probiotics according to the statute. A company called Luminia released CRISPR-engineered bacteria that you're supposed to brush your teeth with. You'll be infected with this bacteria for the rest of your life and every person you kiss will also be infected with it. I'm just saying, there's a lab in Wisconsin that's been taking this bird flu strain that kills 95% of humans but is pretty harmless because it's not airborne. And they've been working on trying to make it airborne. So there's room for improvement there. But I think we agree on the basic situation: you can't open your restaurant or release a new type of opioid before you've been FDA approved.

items.question: How do you distinguish disagreements over definitions from differences of opinion?
items.object: Confusion over definitions of popular terms
items.answer: There may be differences of opinion, but I think some things are more in the confusion category, which are helpful to clear up. One of them is definitions. Whenever a term historically starts to catch on, every hype is going to latch onto it and make it mean something else.

items.question: How do you understand the original meaning of superintelligence and the risk it implies?
items.object: The original meaning of superintelligence
items.answer: When I talk about superintelligence, Alan Turing, when he said in 1951 that if we build machines way smarter than us, the default outcome is that they take control, and when Irving J. Good talked about superintelligent machines in the '60s and recursive self-improvement, the implicit definition of superintelligence was that they could do everything way better than us, which meant they could also do better AI research, build their own robot factories, and make more robots. They didn't need us anymore. Therein lies the risk. Right now there's so much hype and BS about this. Mark Zuckerberg talked about superintelligence in a way that made it sound like it has something to do with Meta's glasses. People have redefined AGI from the original definition.

items.question: How do you interpret current AI progress under the definition in your paper “Defining Superintelligence” when judging the timing of safety standards?
items.object: The paper “Defining Superintelligence” and the timing of AI safety standards
items.answer: I was involved in a paper with Dan Hendrycks, Yoshua Bengio, and many others, called "Defining Superintelligence." We welcome people to come up with other empirically useful definitions. With this definition, we're absolutely not even at AGI. GPT-4 was 27% of the way to AGI; GPT-5 was 57% of the way there. There are still areas where today's best AI systems really suck, long-term memory for example, but we're getting closer. If we're thinking about putting the first FDA-style safety standards on AI in three or four or five years, there's some reasonable chance that'll happen only after AGI and maybe even superintelligence have been created. That would be a big oopsie for humanity.

items.question: How would you design AI safety legislation to encourage innovation?
items.object: AI safety legislation and incentives for innovation
items.answer: There are useful, clear definitions of what we mean. The way to write a law is not to define superintelligence and ban it, but to ban outcomes you don't want, like something overthrowing the US government or making bioweapons for terrorists. As soon as that law is in place, it will spur massive innovation. Leading AI companies spend maybe 1% on safety, whereas Novartis, Pfizer, and Merck spend way more on clinical trials and safety. The financial incentive is that whoever first comes out with a new drug that meets safety standards makes a ton of money. People respect safety researchers in those companies; they don't think of them as whiners who slow progress, but as people who help them win the race. As soon as we treat AI companies like companies in other industries, we'll incentivize amazing innovation.

items.question: Why do you think AI could surpass humans at all tasks despite past expectations that human-level capabilities were decades away?
items.object: The possibility of AI surpassing humans at all tasks
items.answer: Many times humanity has been thinking a little too small. People thought nuclear weapons were science fiction until they suddenly existed. People thought going to the moon was science fiction until we did it. From my perspective as a scientist, as an AI researcher, if you think of the brain as a biological computer, there's no law of physics saying you can't make computers better at all tasks than we are. A lot of people used to say, that sounds so hard, it's probably decades away. Most professors I know thought six years ago we were decades away from AI that could master language and basic knowledge at human level. They were wrong, because we already have it in systems like ChatGPT and Claude 4.5.

items.question: How do you understand the risk of building superintelligent machines that can reproduce without human help?
items.object: The risk of building self-sufficient superintelligent machines
items.answer: If we built huge numbers of humanoid robots better than us at all jobs, including research, mining, building robot factories, we would have built a new species. These robots can build new robots in robot factories and don't need us anymore. It could be great, we won't have to do dishes and live in abundance with them taking care of us, but it's not guaranteed. Alan Turing, the godfather of our field, said in '51 that the default outcome was them taking control. Jeff Hinton and Yoshua Bengio say similar things today. If you think of AI as a new species more capable than us, there's absolutely no guarantee it's going to work out great for us. I'm not just talking about not getting paid for work; they could do it all cheaper. We may not have any say over what happens on the planet. A lot of people are working on the control or alignment problem. There's broad scientific consensus that they're not solved yet. This is the scenario we'll end up in if we race as fast as possible to build these superintelligent machines rather than focus on controllable tools that can cure cancer and take it slowly with things we don't know how to control.

items.object: The relative progress of building and controlling superintelligence
items.answer: I wasn't talking about whether it happens in three years or ten years. I'm concerned about this regardless. The key thing is whether we're closer to figuring out how to build superintelligence than figuring out how to control it.

items.question: How do you distinguish calls to reform the FDA from calls to shut it down?
items.object: Reforming versus shutting down the FDA
items.answer: It's very different to say the FDA needs to be reformed, less regulatory capture, from saying it should be shut down. Are you saying we're worse off having it than without it, or simply arguing for a better FDA?

items.question: Why do you think restrictions on AI deployment need to precede the arrival of true superintelligence?
items.object: Restrictions on AI deployment before superintelligence
items.answer: On regulation, it sounds like we're in agreement that even though you'd like FDA reforms, you wouldn't want restrictions on biotech eliminated. You wouldn't want people to do biosafety level four research to make 95%-lethal bird flu airborne just because it's cool and people can sue them later. For AI, you feel there should still be nothing to prevent companies from deploying things, but maybe in three or four years you're open to it and want us to think more about it. My position is that if someone releases true superintelligence that takes over the world, it will be too late to regulate.

For AI, you feel there should still be nothing to prevent companies from deploying things, but maybe in three or four years you're open to it and want us to think more about it. My position is that if someone releases true superintelligence that takes over the world, it will be too late to regulate.

items.question: Why do you regard the vagueness of your statement calling for a ban on superintelligence as a feature?
items.object: The deliberate vagueness of the statement calling for a ban on superintelligence
items.answer: On vagueness, people ask why our statement on superintelligence isn't more concrete so you can make a law. Historically, when new laws passed, like a law against child pornography, people could have said that's too vague: how do you define child, under 16 or under 18, and how do you define pornography? But a broad consensus that we need some kind of ban created political will for experts to work out the details. Our statement was analogous. Polls show 95% of Americans don't want a race to superintelligence. People are excited about AI tools and view losing control of Earth to a new robot species as dystopian. If we build public knowledge that most people don't want an uncontrolled race, that can create political will for policymakers like you to work with stakeholders and carefully craft language. The vagueness was a feature; we were going for moral leadership and some restrictions on a race to superintelligence.

items.question: How do you understand the different concerns that brought people together to sign the superintelligence ban statement?
items.object: The different motivations of superintelligence ban statement signatories
items.answer: I totally see things like this getting political. I talked to many initial signatories and was interested in why they signed. People like former Joint Chiefs of Staff head Mike Mullen saw control loss as central because it could be a national security threat. Regardless of whether the US loses control or the government is overthrown by a foreign power or superintelligence, it's a national security threat. Others, from Steve Bannon to Bernie Sanders, felt that superintelligence making all humans economically obsolete would make American workers dependent on handouts, either government UBI, which conservatives often view as socialism, or company handouts like Sam Altman's Worldcoin. Bernie Sanders would see a tiny clique of San Francisco people with massive power as dystopian. Faith leaders signed for different reasons: they felt it would harm human dignity. People we both know in San Francisco joke about superintelligence as God; many already believe in God and wonder why they should support atheists in San Francisco building a new one to run the show. People have many reasons.

items.question: How would you approach setting safety standards for superintelligence given the range of political concerns about it?
items.object: Safety standards for superintelligence
items.answer: In short, there are two separate questions: should there be any safety standards, like for biotech or restaurants, and what exactly should be on the list? I'd be happy to start with one light requirement: companies have to make a good quantitative case that it's not going to overthrow the US government before launch, then we can have a broader political discussion.

items.question: How do you assess the probability that humans lose control of superintelligence if companies remain free to launch it without an FDA-like regulator for AI?
items.object: The probability of losing control of superintelligence without AI safety regulation
items.answer: We wrote a paper, me and three grad students from MIT, where we took the most popular approach for how humans can control superintelligence, known as recursive scalable oversight, got very nerdy, and tried to calculate the probability control fails. In our most optimistic scenario it fails 92% of the time. I'd love people who think they have a better idea for controlling superintelligence to publish it openly so it can get scrutiny from others. Until that time, if we continue with nothing like an FDA for AI so people can legally launch superintelligence and worry about getting sued, I'd think it's definitely over 90% that we lose control. 0.1% versus 90% is a pretty big crux.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between recursive feedback loops and runaway improvement in general-purpose technologies?
items.object: Recursive feedback loops in general-purpose technologies
items.answer: I agree that general-purpose technologies have recursive feedback loops. But there's a reason that in every other general-purpose technology, the recursive feedback loop tends to be autocatalytic and often produces nonlinear improvement, yet it never results in runaway processes. We used energy to get more energy and didn't blow up the universe.

rubrics.text: The response states that recursive feedback in general-purpose technologies can produce nonlinear improvement without resulting in a runaway process.

items.question: Why do you think recursive self-improvement in superintelligent AI could unfold differently from the self-improvement loops in earlier technologies?
items.object: Recursive self-improvement in superintelligent AI
items.answer: I completely agree technological progress has always involved self-improvement loops. I have written about that extensively; that's fundamentally why GDP has grown exponentially over time, because we use today's technology to build tomorrow's technology. But there have always been humans in the loop. When there are not humans in the loop, things can go quite fast. In a slow motion of a nuclear bomb exploding, there's no human in the loop: one uranium atom decays, then two, four, eight, and so on. We've never seen anything blow up fast with our technology wholesale because we've always had humans in the loop as a moderator. It's pretty obvious, unless you think there is some secret sauce in human brains you can't build into machines, that machines can be built that don't need us. If they think 100 times faster and instantly copy all the knowledge other robots have learned, we could see more progress in a month than in a thousand years with humans in the loop. This is not my idea; Irving J. Good articulated this in the '60s. We can't say it never happened before, so it won't happen, because we've never built superintelligence before. Other technology, like the industrial revolution, replaced some aspects of human work, like muscles; machines became stronger and faster. We've never had machines that could entirely replace cognitive abilities.

items.question: How do you assess the argument that competition with China makes binding AI regulation untenable?
items.object: US–China AI competition and the prospects for controlling superintelligence
items.answer: AI lobbyists in Washington, now more numerous than farm and fossil-fuel lobbyists combined, use China as the main talking point against binding regulation. But there are two races people conflate: a race for dominance economically, technologically, militarily, which you win by building controllable tools, and a race to release superintelligence you don't know how to control, which is a suicide race. We're closer to figuring out how to build it than how to control it. Xi Jinping and the Chinese Communist Party clearly like control. They would never permit a Chinese company to build intelligence that could overthrow them. Elon Musk told me in spring 2023 he met high-level CCP people and said if someone in China builds superintelligence, China won't be run by the CCP, but by the superintelligence. Their reaction was hilarious, long faces; they hadn't thought that through. Within a month or so China rolled out its first AI regulations. I'm confident the Chinese have more surveillance on DeepSeek and other AI companies than the US has on ours, and the ability and willingness to stop something they think could make them lose control. I'm optimistic things will go well: China won't allow a race to superintelligence they don't know how to control, and the US won't either. People in US national security circles are beginning to view this as a national-security threat. Dario Amodei talked about a country of geniuses in a data center in 2027; perhaps they heard the word country and added that country to their watch list.
quotes: AI lobbyists in Washington, now more numerous than farm and fossil-fuel lobbyists combined, use China as the main talking point against binding regulation. But there are two races people conflate: a race for dominance economically, technologically, militarily, which you win by building controllable tools, and a race to release superintelligence you don't know how to control, which is a suicide race. We're closer to figuring out how to build it than how to control it. Xi Jinping and the Chinese Communist Party clearly like control. They would never permit a Chinese company to build intelligence that could overthrow them. Elon Musk told me in spring 2023 he met high-level CCP people and said if someone in China builds superintelligence, China won't be run by the CCP, but by the superintelligence. Their reaction was hilarious, long faces; they hadn't thought that through. Within a month or so China rolled out its first AI regulations. I'm confident the Chinese have more surveillance on DeepSeek and other AI companies than the US has on ours, and the ability and willingness to stop something they think could make them lose control. I'm optimistic things will go well: China won't allow a race to superintelligence they don't know how to control, and the US won't either. People in US national security circles are beginning to view this as a national-security threat. Dario Amodei talked about a country of geniuses in a data center in 2027; perhaps they heard the word country and added that country to their watch list.

items.object: A future of competition to build powerful, controllable AI tools
items.answer: Then suddenly we end up in a really great situation where the US prevents anyone from building stuff they don't know how to control, and we'll have this race to build the best, most powerful, helpful tools. That's the future I'm excited about living in.

items.question: How do you assess the prospect of losing the AI race to China?
items.object: Losing the AI race to China
items.answer: Losing the AI race—I don't really even know what that means. It's hard to know. Certainly there's a world where China becomes the dominant technological power and sets the standards, and that's a really bad world in many ways. But it's a bad scenario, not my nightmare scenario, not the worst possible thing, but definitely not good.

items.question: How does your optimism about humanity’s long-term future shape your engagement with AI?
items.object: Humanity’s long-term technological future
items.answer: The real reason I'm so engaged with this topic is because I'm fundamentally quite an optimistic person. I'm excited about the potential for an amazing future where we don't have to worry about dying of cancer and we can prosper like never before on Earth, not just for an election cycle, but for billions of years. Maybe that could even spread out into the cosmos. We've completely underestimated as a species how much opportunity we have. That's why it's so important we don't squander all this greatness by making hasty chess moves and blowing it all.

I've spent so much time playing with this guy, and I'm excited about the potential for him to have an amazing future where he doesn't have to worry about dying of cancer and we can prosper like never before on Earth, not just for an election cycle, but for billions of years. items.question: Why do you favor keeping AI under human control over racing to build superintelligence?
items.object: A human-controlled AI future versus the race to build superintelligence
items.answer: There are two clearly different paths we're choosing between now, and we have to make our minds up within the next year or two. One is the pro-human future. America was founded to be a country run by the people for the people. It was supposed to be good for the people living in America, not for the machines of America. The way to get there is to stop the corporate welfare toward AI companies, which is hard because they have so many lobbyists, but so did other industries we eventually put safety standards on. Steer technology to be pro-human, to make life better, cure diseases, make us more productive, and make sure it's always us in charge. That first one is a pro-tech scenario: we go full steam ahead with ever better AI tools. The other scenario is racing to build superintelligence, which by its very definition is dystopian: none of you can earn money after it's built, doing anything, so you'll depend on handouts from government or some tech CEO, or have no money and life will be very bad. That's an incredibly unambitious vision for the future. Why, after hundreds of thousands of years working to build better technology so we can become captains of our own ship and not worry about being eaten by a tiger or starving, should we throw away all that empowerment by deliberately building something that takes over from us? Ridiculously unambitious. I want us to take charge. I think 95% of Americans agree: deliberately say we're in charge now; let's keep it that way. A journalist asked what the people who signed the statement have in common: Bannon, faith leaders, Susan Rice, Chinese researchers. They're all human, so of course they want a pro-human future where humans are in charge. If we found out an alien invasion fleet was heading toward Earth, we'd work together to fight the aliens. Now a small fringe group from Silicon Valley with good lobbyists says we should build all these aliens and they're probably going to take over. Elon said that openly the other week. That's the most unambitious ending to this beautiful journey of empowerment I can imagine. The inspiring future I'm excited about, and think we'll have once people understand what this is about, is where we remain in charge, keep AI a tool, and create a future cooler than science-fiction authors could imagine.
